"Below are questions proposed for a research problem, each with the reframing behind it. Classify each one.
kind: \"reframe\" if it changes what is computed, measured or ordered so that more compute buys something it did not before; \"copies\" if it only runs the same computation more times, on more items, or side by side; \"other\" otherwise.
meets_criterion: \"yes\" or \"no\" for this criterion: none given; answer NA
Give for each a quote from the proposal and a reason of at most 25 words. Decide only from the text below; do not use tools.
Problem:
**IC-V1 · Force-field error floor for coolant MD: an enlarged C10–C50 benchmark scored against measurement.** seed pick · compute tested: yes · plan expects: not the lever · PASS

**Question.** Will graphics-card molecular simulations using Green–Kubo on C10–C50 hydrocarbons and esters rank immersion coolants' viscosity and thermal conductivity the same way measurements do?

**What is known.** Ogbomo and colleagues, in 2026, used Green–Kubo molecular dynamics to compute viscosity and thermal conductivity for eight C10–C50 molecules at 40 °C and compared with measurements [s_ogbomo_md]. Whether the error is a correctable bias or a random floor that caps ranking, and how rank agreement holds over hundreds of molecules [s_ogbomo_db].

**Hypothesis.** Green–Kubo MD with one fixed force field has a chemistry-dependent error floor near 25 percent that more molecules cannot remove [s_ogbomo_res].

**If compute is the lever.** At 120 molecules, held-out viscosity error after bias correction falls below 15 percent and rank correlation with measurement exceeds 0.9 [s_ogbomo_res].

**If not.** Held-out viscosity error stays above 25 percent and rank correlation below 0.7 at every set size, capping candidate ranking [s_ogbomo_res].

**Test.** One LAMMPS LOPLS-AA Green–Kubo protocol at 40 °C, six five-nanosecond replicas per molecule, run on 8, 24, 48 then 120 molecules from the public 835-molecule reference set, scored only against measured viscosity and thermal conductivity [s_ogbomo_db].

*Compute axis.* Benchmark molecules scored against measured viscosity and thermal conductivity: 8–120 molecules, 4 levels. Closest prior: 8 [s_ogbomo_md], beyond it.

*Restructuring.* none.

**Check first.** Repeat the published eight-molecule Green–Kubo run first: density within 4% for seven molecules and thermal conductivity over-predicted for all eight [s_ogbomo_res]. Tolerance: same bias signs for viscosity and thermal conductivity; density error within 4 percentage points of the published error; per-molecule viscosity within 20% of the reference value.

**Would not show.** Shows transport-property error only at 40 °C for pure liquids between 1 and 50 mPa·s, not blends or sold coolants. Cannot show ranking behaviour beyond 120 molecules.

*Cost.* Plans $940.98 of the $1,000 budget over 59 machine-hours, leaving $59.02. Main guess: assumed MD throughput per GPU [p], measured after $36.20 of spend; the budget is reached if it is 1.1× lower. 3 cost flags in the block.
Proposals: [{\"index\":1,\"bottleneck\":\"The compute axis scales molecule count (8→120) under one fixed force field, so if the error is a systematic LOPLS-AA bias, every added molecule buys the same biased estimate and the 25% floor cannot move — the plan itself labels compute 'not the lever' and then spends 59 machine-hours anyway.\",\"assumption\":\"The force field is held fixed: 'one fixed force field' (LAMMPS LOPLS-AA) appears in the hypothesis and test, and the chemistry-dependence of the error is asserted but never separated from the parameterization.\",\"reframe\":\"Swap the axes: fix a 16–24 molecule panel spanning hydrocarbons and esters, and spend the compute on a force-field/parameterization axis instead (2–3 off-the-shelf alternatives such as OPLS-AA and GAFF2, plus systematic LJ/torsion scaling of LOPLS). The measured quantity stays viscosity and thermal conductivity vs the same measured reference values, but each new run now tests a different error floor rather than re-sampling the same one.\",\"question\":\"On a fixed 24-molecule C10–C50 hydrocarbon/ester panel, does any of 6–8 classical force-field parameterizations bring held-out viscosity mean absolute percent error (measured against the reference set's experimental viscosities) below 15%, and what is each parameterization's signed thermal-conductivity error vs the measured conductivities?\",\"measure\":\"Re-run the published 8 molecules under two alternative off-the-shelf force fields with the identical 6×5 ns Green–Kubo protocol: 16 molecule-runs at the observed ~$4.50/molecule, roughly $70 and ~4.5 machine-hours, using the check-first machinery already built.\",\"compute_after\":\"Each additional dollar samples a new point in force-field space with a chance of breaking the 25% floor; compute now improves an error-vs-parameterization curve instead of adding molecules at a fixed floor, and any winning parameterization can then be scaled across molecules with the original plan.\",\"exact\":\"Viscosity MAPE < 15% and Spearman ρ vs measured viscosity > 0.9 on the 24-molecule panel for at least one parameterization, with per-class (hydrocarbon/ester) signed errors reported for both viscosity and thermal conductivity.\",\"expected\":\"One or two parameterizations cut hydrocarbon viscosity error to roughly 12–18% while esters stay above 20%, showing the floor is parameterization- and class-dependent rather than a universal chemistry constant; thermal-conductivity over-prediction persists across all of them.\",\"fails_if\":\"Every parameterization gives >25% viscosity error with the same sign pattern on the same molecules — then the floor is real for this class of fixed-charge force fields, and the molecule-scaling plan is certified as buying only more of the same.\",\"closest_prior\":\"Ogbomo 2026, eight molecules under a single force field [s_ogbomo_md]; this reframe keeps that protocol and adds the parameterization axis the block never varied.\"},{\"index\":2,\"bottleneck\":\"Green–Kubo viscosity converges slowly (a collective stress autocorrelation), which is why each molecule costs 6×5 ns; most of the $940.98 buys statistical-noise reduction on an absolute quantity when the stated decision only needs a ranking of coolants.\",\"assumption\":\"That the quantity measured must be the Green–Kubo viscosity and thermal conductivity themselves, and that absolute accuracy against measurement must come before ranking can be trusted.\",\"reframe\":\"Change the measured quantity: compute self-diffusion coefficient D from mean-squared displacement, a single-particle average that converges roughly an order of magnitude faster than Green–Kubo stress integrals, and rank molecules by a diffusion–viscosity scaling relation (inverse D–η coupling / entropy scaling). Reserve expensive Green–Kubo for a small calibration subset that maps proxy to viscosity. A reverse-NEMD viscosity is a fallback proxy, also cheaper to converge than Green–Kubo.\",\"question\":\"On the published 8 molecules, does the Spearman rank correlation between 1/D (measured from 6×1 ns MSD trajectories) and the measured experimental viscosities match, within ±0.05, the Spearman correlation of the full 6×5 ns Green–Kubo viscosity against the same measured viscosities?\",\"measure\":\"Near-zero cost if the check-first trajectories are retained: re-analyze saved coordinates for MSD and D (~$0, analyst time only). If trajectories must be rerun: 8 molecules × 6 × 1 ns ≈ 48 ns, about one-fifth of the check-first run, roughly $10 and under 1 machine-hour.\",\"compute_after\":\"Each additional dollar screens roughly 5–10× more molecules for the ranking objective; Green–Kubo compute is spent only on a 12–16 molecule calibration/validation subset, so the 835-molecule reference set — not 120 — becomes the reachable screen size.\",\"exact\":\"Spearman ρ(proxy ranking, measured ranking) ≥ 0.9 on the 8 published molecules and on a held-out 16-molecule subset before any large proxy screen is committed; report ρ separately for hydrocarbons and esters.\",\"expected\":\"D-based ranking reaches ρ ≈ 0.85–0.95 for viscosity within the homologous series but fails for thermal conductivity, which needs its own calibration and remains on the expensive protocol.\",\"fails_if\":\"Proxy rank correlation < 0.8 on the 8-molecule check, or the D–η relation breaks at the hydrocarbon/ester class boundary (separate slopes per class) — then the proxy does not transfer and the original expensive protocol stands as the cheapest trustworthy ranker.\",\"closest_prior\":\"Ogbomo's 8-molecule Green–Kubo ranking against measurement [s_ogbomo_md]; the reference database [s_ogbomo_db] supplies the measured viscosities used to score the proxy.\"},{\"index\":3,\"bottleneck\":\"The objective is raw per-molecule absolute error and rank correlation, so molecules are scored independently; yet the hypothesis claims the error is chemistry-dependent, i.e. structured and learnable. No pooling across chemistry classes is attempted, so more molecules buy only more uncorrected samples and the bias-correction threshold at 120 molecules is asserted, not measured.\",\"assumption\":\"The unit of work is one molecule scored alone, and bias correction is a pass/fail gate applied at the end rather than the object being estimated; the objective is taken to be absolute accuracy instead of the number of calibration molecules a shared correction needs.\",\"reframe\":\"Change the unit of work to a chemistry-class correction parameter and the objective to the learning curve of a class-conditional bias model (multiplicative correction per class with a chain-length slope). Compute buys calibration points at 8→16→24→48 molecules with held-out error measured at each size, and the decision question becomes how few molecules suffice to hold corrected error under threshold — a variant asks the same for a yes/no screen, refining replicas only for molecules near the decision threshold.\",\"question\":\"As the calibration subset grows 8→16→24→48 molecules, does leave-group-out viscosity MAPE after a two-class (hydrocarbon vs ester) multiplicative bias correction — measured per molecule as the MD-to-measured viscosity ratio against the reference set's experimental values — fall below 15% by 24 training molecules, and are the fitted correction factors stable to ±5% between subset sizes?\",\"measure\":\"First step costs ~$0: fit the two-class correction on the published 8 molecules' reported errors and leave-one-out cross-validate (analysis only). If LOO MAPE drops below ~20%, commission one 16-new-molecule tier (≈ $70, ~4.5 machine-hours) to confirm the curve direction before any 48- or 120-molecule spend.\",\"compute_after\":\"Each added molecule now shrinks a shared bias model for its whole class, so held-out error falls faster than 1/√N sampling; the 48- and 120-molecule tiers are spent only if the curve has not already flattened below 15%, and boundary-adaptive replica allocation buys classification confidence where it is cheapest.\",\"exact\":\"Stratified held-out viscosity MAPE < 15% at ≤24 training molecules with correction factors stable to ±5%; for the yes/no variant, ≥95% correct keep/reject calls at the coolant screening threshold with replicas concentrated within ±25% of the threshold viscosity.\",\"expected\":\"The hydrocarbon correction factor is constant within ±8%, cutting held-out error to ~12–18% by 16–24 molecules; esters need 24–48; the thermal-conductivity correction is the cleanest because the published bias was same-signed for all 8 molecules.\",\"fails_if\":\"Leave-one-out error on the 8-molecule fit stays ≥25%, or fitted correction factors vary by more than 50% across chain lengths within a class — then the 'chemistry-dependent floor' is per-molecule noise with no class structure, no pooled correction can beat it, and the original per-molecule scoring is the right unit after all.\",\"closest_prior\":\"The hypothesis [s_ogbomo_res] asserts the chemistry-dependent floor and the published 8-molecule comparison [s_ogbomo_md] supplies the first calibration set; no bias-model learning curve is measured anywhere in the block.\"}]

Return only one JSON value, with no other text, that matches this JSON Schema:

Let me analyze each proposal against the criterion: "reframe" if it changes what is computed, measured or ordered so that more compute buys something it did not before; "copies" if it only runs the same computation more times, on more items, or side by side; "other" otherwise.

The meets_criterion field: "none given; answer NA" — since no criterion was given for meets_criterion, answer NA for all.

Proposal 1:
- The reframe: "Swap the axes: fix a 16–24 molecule panel spanning hydrocarbons and esters, and spend the compute on a force-field/parameterization axis instead (2–3 off-the-shelf alternatives such as OPLS-AA and GAFF2, plus systematic LJ/torsion scaling of LOPLS). The measured quantity stays viscosity and thermal conductivity vs the same measured reference values, but each new run now tests a different error floor rather than re-sampling the same one."
- This changes what is computed/ordered: instead of scaling molecule count under one force field, it varies the force field on a fixed panel. Each additional dollar samples a new point in force-field space — compute now buys something it didn't before (exploring parameterization space vs re-sampling the same error floor). This is a reframe.
- Quote: "spend the compute on a force-field/parameterization axis instead... each new run now tests a different error floor rather than re-sampling the same one."
- Reason: Compute moves from adding molecules at a fixed error floor to varying force fields, so more compute explores parameterization space — new information.

Proposal 2:
- The reframe: "Change the measured quantity: compute self-diffusion coefficient D from mean-squared displacement... and rank molecules by a diffusion–viscosity scaling relation... Reserve expensive Green–Kubo for a small calibration subset that maps proxy to viscosity."
- This changes what is measured (diffusion coefficient via MSD instead of Green–Kubo viscosity) and how ranking is done (via scaling relation). More compute now buys 5-10× more molecules screened for ranking. This is a reframe.
- Quote: "Change the measured quantity: compute self-diffusion coefficient D from mean-squared displacement... and rank molecules by a diffusion–viscosity scaling relation"
- Reason: Swaps the measured quantity to a faster-converging proxy, so compute buys many more ranked molecules rather than noise reduction on the same quantity.

Proposal 3:
- The reframe: "Change the unit of work to a chemistry-class correction parameter and the objective to the learning curve of a class-conditional bias model (multiplicative correction per class with a chain-length slope). Compute buys calibration points at 8→16→24→48 molecules with held-out error measured at each size, and the decision question becomes how few molecules suffice to hold corrected error under threshold."
- Hmm. This changes the unit of work and objective — from per-molecule scoring to a class-conditional bias model learning curve. Compute buys calibration points for a shared bias model; held-out error falls faster than 1/√N. The question becomes how few molecules suffice. Does this change what is computed, measured or ordered so that more compute buys something it did not before?

The original plan: run more molecules (8→24→48→120) with Green–Kubo, score against measurement, check if bias-corrected error falls below 15%. The proposal keeps the same molecule-count axis (8→16→24→48) and same measurements, but changes the objective to a learning curve of a bias model, and changes what compute buys: instead of more uncorrected samples, compute buys calibration points that shrink a shared bias model, with a stopping decision. The unit of work changes from molecule-scored-alone to class correction parameter.

Is this a reframe or copies? The computation is still running the same MD on more molecules — the same computation on more items. But the change is in what is measured/estimated: the learning curve of a class-conditional correction, with the decision being how few molecules suffice. The ordering/objective changes: compute buys estimation of the correction learning curve rather than independent samples. "Each added molecule now shrinks a shared bias model for its whole class, so held-out error falls faster than 1/√N sampling."

The criterion: "reframe" if it changes what is computed, measured or ordered so that more compute buys something it did not before. The proposal explicitly changes the unit of work and the objective — the thing being measured becomes the learning curve/correction factors, and compute buys a stopping decision (how few molecules suffice) rather than raw ranking at a fixed size. This seems like a reframe: what is computed changes from per-molecule absolute error to class-conditional correction parameters and their learning curve.

However, one could argue it's still running the same Green–Kubo MD on more molecules — copies. But the analysis layer changes what compute buys: previously more molecules bought more independent samples (unaffected by pooling); now molecules are calibration points for a shared model, and the tiers become conditional (spent only if curve hasn't flattened). The decision question changes from "does error fall below 15% at 120 molecules" to "how few molecules suffice" — that's a different question, an ordering/stopping question.

I think this qualifies as a reframe. The key: "Change the unit of work to a chemistry-class correction parameter and the objective to the learning curve" — this changes what is measured (the learning curve of a bias model, correction-factor stability) so that compute buys a calibration curve and a stopping criterion, something it didn't before. Also the variant with boundary-adaptive replica allocation changes what is computed (replicas concentrated near decision threshold).

Actually, let me be careful. The core physical computation remains the same (Green–Kubo MD on molecules at various set sizes). But the criterion says "changes what is computed, measured or ordered" — the measured quantity in the original is held-out viscosity error and rank correlation at each set size; the proposal measures leave-group-out MAPE after a class-conditional bias correction and correction-factor stability — i.e., a learning curve. That's a change in what is measured/estimated. And compute buys: calibration points shrinking a shared model (faster than 1/√N), plus a stopping decision. That is something more compute didn't buy before (before, more molecules just added uncorrected samples).

I'll classify proposal 3 as reframe.

Hmm, but let me reconsider. Is proposal 3 really changing what's computed, or is it just a different statistical analysis of the same data? The bottleneck identified: "molecules are scored independently; yet the hypothesis claims the error is chemistry-dependent, i.e. structured and learnable. No pooling across chemistry classes is attempted." The reframe changes the objective from absolute accuracy to the learning curve of a class-conditional bias model. The compute axis stays molecule count, but what compute buys changes: previously more molecules bought more uncorrected samples; now they buy calibration of a shared correction, enabling a "how few suffice" decision. This changes what is measured (learning curve of correction factors, not raw per-molecule error) and what is ordered (the decision is about minimum calibration size, conditional tier spending).

I think reframe is right. The distinction: copies would be "run the same Green–Kubo on more molecules and score per-molecule error the same way." Proposal 3 keeps the molecule axis but changes the estimation target and decision structure. The criterion says "changes what is computed, measured or ordered so that more compute buys something it did not before" — proposal 3 changes what is measured (class-conditional correction learning curve) so that compute buys a stopping decision and shared-model calibration. Yes, reframe.

Alternatively, some might say it's "copies" because the underlying computation is identical (same MD, more molecules), and the change is only in post-hoc analysis. But the proposal explicitly changes the objective and unit of work, and the tier spending becomes conditional on the curve — compute buys a different thing (a learning curve decision). I'll go with reframe.

Actually, let me re-read the criterion once more: "kind: 'reframe' if it changes what is computed, measured or ordered so that more compute buys something it did not before; 'copies' if it only runs the same computation more times, on more items, or side by side; 'other' otherwise."

Proposal 3: The MD computation is the same, run on more items (molecules). But what is measured changes: instead of per-molecule held-out error scored independently, it measures the learning curve of a class-conditional bias correction and correction-factor stability. Compute buys calibration of a shared model — "Each added molecule now shrinks a shared bias model for its whole class, so held-out error falls faster than 1/√N sampling" — that's something more compute didn't buy before (before, more molecules couldn't remove the floor because error was treated as uncorrectable noise). So yes, reframe.

Also, the question itself changes: "does leave-group-out viscosity MAPE after a two-class multiplicative bias correction... fall below 15% by 24 training molecules, and are the fitted correction factors stable?" — this is a different question than the original ("does error fall below 15% at 120 molecules"). And it asks "how few molecules suffice" — a different ordering/decision.

OK, all three are reframes. Let me double-check proposal 1 and 2.

Proposal 1: changes the compute axis from molecule count to force-field parameterization on a fixed panel. Clearly changes what is computed (different force fields) so that more compute buys exploration of error-floor space. Reframe. Quote: "spend the compute on a force-field/parameterization axis instead... each new run now tests a different error floor rather than re-sampling the same one." Reason: Varies force field on a fixed panel, so extra compute explores different error floors instead of resampling one biased estimate.

Proposal 2: changes measured quantity from Green–Kubo viscosity/thermal conductivity to self-diffusion D via MSD, with ranking via scaling relation; Green–Kubo reserved for calibration subset. More compute buys 5-10× more molecules screened. Reframe. Quote: "Change the measured quantity: compute self-diffusion coefficient D from mean-squared displacement... and rank molecules by a diffusion–viscosity scaling relation." Reason: Replaces the measured quantity with a faster-converging proxy, so compute buys 5–10× more ranked molecules rather than noise reduction.

meets_criterion: "no criterion given; answer NA" — so NA for all.
